entities.name: Kalila and Demna
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Kalila and Dimna is one of the most widely translated and influential collections of instructive fables in world literary history. Originating in Sanskrit as the Panchatantra (c. 3rd century BCE – 3rd century CE), the work was translated into Pahlavi (Middle Persian) by the physician Borzuya for Sassanid King Khosrow I Anushirvan (r. 531–579 CE), and from Pahlavi into Arabic by Ibn al-Muqaffa' c. 750 CE. This Arabic version — Kalila wa-Dimna — became the definitive text from which dozens of translations proliferated across the Islamic world and into medieval Europe.

The collection is organized as a frame narrative in which the two jackals Kalila and Dimna discuss the political relationships between animals that serve as allegories for human statecraft. The fables address rulers, advisers, enemies, friends, and the treacheries of court life — offering a sophisticated manual of political wisdom in animal form. Ibn al-Muqaffa's Arabic version was itself a landmark of Arabic prose style and helped establish adab (literary culture) as a genre.

The influence of Kalila and Dimna on world literature is extraordinary. Translated into Syriac, Greek, Hebrew, Latin, Old Spanish, Persian, and eventually most European languages, its fables seeded Western fable traditions — including those of La Fontaine. The Panchatantra source material is considered a primary ancestor of Aesop's Fables via Greek intermediaries. Its distribution from India through Persia, the Islamic world, and Europe makes it one of the most globally traveled literary works in history.
